Error terms for integral approximations are not as straightforward because, in each case, the quantity being approximated depends on {{MATH:6}}. Changing {{MATH:7}} in the integration formula also changes the quantity being approximated. This is true of each formula in table {{REF:8}}. The trapezoidal rule is as good an example as any. The left hand side, the quantity being approximated, is {{MATH:9}}, so smaller {{MATH:10}} means approximating the integral over a smaller interval. The non-adaptive composite trapezoidal rule gives a slightly better estimate with essentially the same amount of computation. But remember, it is not necessarily efficiency we are after. It is automatic error estimates. The adaptive trapezoidal rule does something the conventional composite trapezoidal rule does not. It monitors itself for accuracy, so when the routine completes, you not only get an estimate, but you can have some confidence in its accuracyeven when you have no way to calculate the integral exactly for comparison.
